headline: Proves that a Banach space with nontrivial Markov type is superreflexive, answering a question of Naor.
scope: Every real Banach space with Markov type p for some p greater than 1.
plain: Markov type measures how far a random walk can drift when its positions are mapped into a space of vectors. Superreflexivity means the space has an equivalent norm with round, uniformly curved balls. It was known that superreflexive spaces have nontrivial Markov type. This paper proves the converse for real Banach spaces, and Lean checks the result. So nontrivial Markov type and superreflexivity are the same property.
doesNot: This does not cover general metric spaces. The theorem is stated for real Banach spaces only.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Assaf Naor, who asked the question in his survey of the Ribe program
scorecard.significanceWhy: It completes a metric characterization of superreflexivity that the Ribe program had left open, with a Lean check.

explanation:
Flip a fair coin and step one unit left or right on the number line. After 100 steps, the average squared distance from the start is exactly 100. So a typical walker is only about 10 units away, not 100. Random walks in straight-line spaces drift like the square root of time.

Markov type turns this into a test for a space of vectors. A Banach space is a space of vectors with a norm, a rule for length, in which limits behave well. Take a Markov chain, a random walk on finitely many states that moves by fixed chances. Call it stationary and reversible if it looks the same run forward or backward. Map its states to vectors by any function f. Look at the p-th power of the distance moved, averaged over the walk. The space has Markov type p with constant K if, after t steps, this average is at most K^p times t times the one-step average. Keith Ball introduced this idea to study how maps extend between spaces[3].

A Banach space is superreflexive if it has an equivalent norm that is uniformly convex. Uniformly convex means the midpoint of two far-apart unit vectors is clearly shorter than one. Bourgain showed earlier that such spaces are exactly those that cannot hold large binary trees with small distortion[4]. Naor, Peres, Schramm and Sheffield showed that suitably smooth norms give Markov type[5]. So every superreflexive space has nontrivial Markov type, meaning Markov type for some p above 1. Naor asked whether the converse holds[6]. One obstacle is that a weaker test fails. Rademacher type, which controls sums with random signs, does not force superreflexivity[7].

The paper proves the converse: every real Banach space with Markov type p for some p above 1 is superreflexive[1]. The proof argues by contradiction[8]. If the space is not superreflexive, it builds a special norm on finite lists of numbers. In that norm, adding neighbouring entries together never makes a list longer[9]. For each time n, it then builds a reversible walk whose steps all have length 1. With chance at least 3/20, the sum of its first n steps has length at least n/24[2]. The 3/20 comes from 1/4 minus 1/10. The walk reaches a reduced length of at least n/4 with chance at least 1/4. It fails a technical condition with chance at most 1/10[10]. Then dividing n/4 by 6 gives n/24.

Here is why that breaks Markov type 2. The average squared length after n steps is at least 3/20 times (n/24) squared. For n = 384,000, n/24 is 16,000. Then 3/20 times 16,000 squared is 38,400,000, which is 100 times n. Markov type 2 says, roughly, that this average stays below K squared times n. Here K squared would have to be at least n divided by 3,840. As n grows, no fixed K works.

How sure is this? Lean, a computer proof checker, has a formal statement of the full result. It says nontrivial Markov type holds exactly when the space has an equivalent uniformly convex norm. So the paper proves this, as far as the Lean statement matches the paper. No specialist review is published.
hypeCheck: Major and Lean-checked. It settles Naor's question for real Banach spaces, not for general metric spaces. No specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: A space of vectors with a length rule, called a norm, in which limits of sequences behave well.
A rule that gives each vector a length, with the usual triangle rule.
A random walk on a set of states where each move depends only on the current state.
A chain whose statistics stay the same over time and look the same run backward.
A bound saying a walk mapped into the space drifts no faster than a fixed power law in time.
A norm where the midpoint of two far-apart unit vectors is shorter than 1 by a fixed margin.
A Banach space that has an equivalent uniformly convex norm.
A bound on the length of sums of vectors with independent random plus or minus signs.
